note: Proposed, not sealed. Written by the willow fleet seat while closing the G2-conventions-nestor bite of the fleet loop plan (Wave 2: every repo carries tests/test_fleet_conventions.py whose rules are read from the published document, `reconciler conventions --json`, never restated). Three choices, each argued Socratically against the repo's own discipline rather than defaulted.

decisions.question: The fleet's convention set now has one home, willow-reconciler 0.6.0's `reconciler conventions --json`. tests/test_fleet_conventions.py must read its rules from that document. Should Nestor (a) add `willow-reconciler>=0.6.0` to the dev extra and `from reconciler.conventions import conventions`, or (b) vendor the document as tests/fleet_conventions.json with a sha256 pin and an optional live-equality check when `reconciler` is importable?
decisions.commitment: (b). tests/fleet_conventions.json is the byte-for-byte output of `reconciler conventions --json` from willow-reconciler 0.6.0 (2301 bytes, sha256 8c2ba122a7100141200d8c76ad086339f984446ab7e90dd9c27a092dbf7f5335, which is also the digest the fleet plan named for that version). The test pins the file to that digest and names the source version; a planted one-key edit is shown to change the digest; and when `reconciler.conventions` is importable on the seat, `conventions()` must equal the vendored document (skipped, not passed, where it is not importable). Nothing is added to pyproject.toml, lint-pins.txt, or CI's install lines.
decisions.why: A new test-time dependency is a real decision in this repo: lint-pins.txt pins every tool CI runs and lint-pins-check.sh refuses on drift; dep-audit.sh audits the resolved environment and fails on any advisory; CI's test job installs `.[keys]` plus pytest and nothing else, so option (a) would either add willow-reconciler (and its transitive set) to the audited surface and a workflow install line, or leave the test skipping on CI, which is the vacuous pass the whole bite exists to forbid. The document is a few hundred bytes that changes only when the fleet's conventions change, and the failure mode of a vendored copy, going stale, is exactly what the pin plus live-equality check turns into a failing test: a bump upstream is either re-vendored and re-pinned by name, or the seat that has the new reconciler sees the mismatch. The recommendation in the bite was (b) for the same reasons; the decision store had nothing on record either way.

decisions.question: `contributing_must_name_test_command` needs one command to hold CONTRIBUTING.md to. CONTRIBUTING's setup and gate table named `python -m pytest -q`; AGENTS.md's gate table names `bash scripts/ci-test.sh full`; CI's test job runs `pytest -n auto --dist loadgroup`. Which is the test command, and does CONTRIBUTING change?
decisions.commitment: `bash scripts/ci-test.sh` (held as the script's name, so a lane argument after it still counts). CONTRIBUTING.md's gate table now names `bash scripts/ci-lint.sh && bash scripts/ci-test.sh full` for the code and mixed rows, the same command AGENTS.md's table carries, with a sentence saying the two tables must not disagree and what the lanes are. The setup block's `python -m pytest -q` smoke run stays: it is a first-run check, not the gate.
decisions.why: The two tables disagreed, and CONTRIBUTING is the one that calls itself 'the single path from clone to merged PR'. ci-test.sh exists so that installing an optional extra cannot enlarge a run and so the local gate is the same collection CI runs (`-n auto --dist loadgroup`); `python -m pytest -q` is the same collection without those guarantees, which is why AGENTS.md moved to the script and CONTRIBUTING had not followed. Holding the test to the script rather than to the bare pytest line makes CONTRIBUTING name the gate a contributor actually owes, and the plant shows that naming a different test command does not satisfy the rule. The published rule was not wrong for Nestor; CONTRIBUTING was stale against Nestor's own AGENTS.md.

decisions.question: `required_config_comments` requires `$comment-hidden-rule` and `$comment-what-cuts-a-release` in release-please-config.json. Nestor's config carries its reasoning under three other `$comment-*` keys (tag-format, no-extra-files, first-bump) and neither required one. Is the rule wrong for Nestor, or does the config gain the two comments?
decisions.commitment: The config gains both, written for this repo: the hidden rule names what `pip install nestor-meaning` delivers and cites jeles v0.4.1; the what-cuts-a-release comment names the closed un-hidden set, cites willow-mcp 2.1.5, says that pr-title.yml reads the list from this file, and gives #292 as the ordinary case. The three existing comments stay. A sixth real-tree check holds the config's un-hidden set to the published `release_cutting_types`, beside the hidden-set check, because pr-title.yml enforces exactly that set from this file.
decisions.why: The rule (fleet plan decision 4) is that the reasoning lives beside the setting it explains so the hidden set cannot be edited without reading why it is what it is; Nestor's config already practised that for three other settings and simply predated the two named keys. The substance was true here, the names were missing, and a test that reads the document cannot honour a comment under a different name without restating the rule, which is the thing the bite forbids. Adding the comments is a config edit under `.github`-adjacent files, ships no different wheel, and is carried by a `test:` commit that cuts no release, as the comment it adds says it should not.
